title: TA8-03367
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XX XXXX XX, (the claimant), a citizen of the People's Republic of China (China), claims refugee protection pursuant to section 96 and subsection 97 (1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act1 (IRPA). Allegations
The claimant alleges the following.

After marriage in 1996, the claimant gave birth to a son. The claimant's relationship with her husband had begun to deteriorate during her pregnancy and the relationship deteriorated even further after the birth of their baby. The claimant and her husband began living with her in-laws in 2003. Because of the isolation and lack of love and warmth over such an extended period of time, the claimant accepted a conversation with a friend regarding Christianity and the Bible in XXXX 2007. After several conversations with her friend, the claimant began attending an underground church in China on XXXX, 2007. Through the claimant's effort, she was able to change her husband's attitude towards her and happiness and laughter came into their family. On XXXX 2007 the claimant's house church was raided by the Public Security Bureau (PSB) and the claimant escaped and went into hiding. Two days later, the PSB came to the claimant's home to look for her and told the claimant's husband that she must surrender herself to them. When the PSB came more frequently to her home to look for her, the claimant realized that she had to flee China and with the support of an agent, left China and came to Canada on XXXX, 2008. Determination
The panel is guided by section 106 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act which states:

The Refugee Protection Division must take into account, with respect to the credibility of a claimant, whether the claimant possesses acceptable documentation establishing identity, and if not, whether they have provided a reasonable explanation for the lack of documentation or have taken reasonable steps to obtain the documentation.

Furthermore, Rule 7 of the Refugee Protection Division Rules states: The claimant must provide acceptable documents establishing identity and other elements of the claim. A claimant who does not provide acceptable documents must explain why they were not provided and what steps were taken to obtain them.

In assessing the authenticity of the claimant's documents, the panel is guided by the Federal Court in Sertkaya2 which asserts that it is open for the Board to consider the authenticity of documentary evidence, and the ability of the claimant to obtain and use fraudulent documents. The panel is also mindful of the Federal Court decision in Rasheed3 whish asserts that the basic rule in Canadian law is that foreign documents (whether they establish identity or not of a claimant) purporting to be issued by a competent foreign public official, should be accepted as evidence of their content unless the Board has some valid reason to doubt their authenticity. The panel also notes that documentary evidence reveals that a wide variety of fraudulent Chinese documents are available to refugee claimants, particularly through snakeheads who facilitate their claims. In the context of the above and below findings and case law, the panel gives little weight to these documents in terms of establishing the claimant's identity Analysis

The determinative issue in regard to this claim is the credibility of the claimant's oral testimony, Personal Information Form (PIF)4 narrative and amendments, and the CIC Refugee Intake Record of Examination.5 Identity
The claimant's identity, as a national of China, is not established by the Resident Identity Card (RIC) presented at the hearing, and other identity documents submitted. Resident Identity Card (RIC)

The panel questioned the authenticity of the Resident of Identity Card (RIC) presented at the hearing because of the address of residence listed on the card, the claimant's inability to speak about issuance procedures, and her lack of knowledge about information included on the RIC.

The claimant produced into evidence an alleged valid RIC,6 of the Peoples Republic of China, issued on XXXX, 2005. The claimant's address on this Ric was XXXX, XXXX XXXX, XXXX, XXXX XXXX, XXXX. The claimant, according to testimony and information submitted in her Personal Information Form (PIF)7, had not lived at this address since 2003, and the panel draws a negative inference from this inconsistency. Counsel, in her submissions, stated that the RIC was never intended as a confirmation of address. The panel disagrees. It is reasonable to expect that when a RIC is issued, the address listed on the RIC will be an accurate address for the owner of the card at the time the RIC is issued. The claimant had to present a Hukou when allegedly making application to replace her previous RIC, and the Hukou8 allegedly presented to the Public Security Bureau (PSB) did not accurately represent the claimant's address. The panel draws a negative inference regarding the claimant's credibility for allegedly presenting an inaccurate or fraudulent document, the Hukou, to the PSB. It is reasonable to expect that the PSB, when issuing a Resident Identity Card (RIC), would want the actual address where the claimant resided as a means of locating her, if necessary, for any number of reasons.

The claimant stated that she was issued her first RIC at the age of 18, in 1987 and that this RIC was good for 10 years. When asked when her second RIC was issued, she said "it is the newest one." The panel asked if she had a RIC before 2005, the date of the RIC that was submitted in evidence for the hearing, and the claimant said she forgot. The claimant stated that she had been issued three RICs during her stay in China, and that the second one was issued in 1996 or 1997, and correctly stated that this RIC was valid for 20 years. The panel draws a negative inference from this evolving testimony, corrected only by a prompt from the panel.

The claimant, when asked to describe the process for acquiring her new RIC, stated that she took a photograph and her Hukou book and had someone to help to acquire her RIC. When asked if the PSB took her picture, the claimant changed her testimony, and said that the PSB came to the village to get her picture and the claimant apologized for not saying this before. When asked who came to the village, she hesitated and gave no answer for over one minute. The panel draws a negative inference from this evolving testimony and inaccurate description for acquiring a RIC. The claimant's testimony is inconsistent with our documentation regarding the acquisition of a RIC9 and the panel draws a negative inference. Our documentation indicates that a person must appear themselves at the PSB office with their Hukou. Their picture is taken by the PSB at this time, and a fee is paid.

The claimant was asked to describe what information was on the face of her new RIC and she said a photograph and an address. When the claimant was asked if there was anything else, she stated an address and the date, but could not describe which date. The claimant was told by the panel that the additional information,10 included on the face of the RIC was: gender, ethnicity, date of birth, and ID number. The claimant said yes and then stated "I can not recall." She then stated there was a design on the back but could not remember what the design was. The design on the reverse side of the card is the Chinese national emblem. The claimant has nine years of formal education and presented well at the hearing. The panel draws a negative inference from the claimant's lack of knowledge about the primary identification card in China. It is reasonable to expect that the claimant would have a clear knowledge of the information on the RIC, as it is necessary for almost every function in China. The RIC presented as evidence does not appear to be fraudulent, but according to our documentation,11 RICs can be obtained fraudulently.

Because of credibility issues outlined regarding the claimant's Hukou, outlined later in these reasons, and the claimant's lack of knowledge about the RIC and its issuance, the claimant has not satisfied the panel that she was a resident of China at the times indicated in her testimony and PIF. The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, the RIC presented in evidence today was not issued to the claimant. The panel also questions the validity of the documents issued as evidence, at this refugee hearing, regarding the claimant's identity and finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the documents are fraudulent, or fraudulently obtained. Hukou

The claimant presented three Hukous as evidence for the hearing. These Hukou where issued over 10 years ago and according to the inconsistencies between testimony and evidence presented, do not accurately reflect the alleged residences of the claimant. According to our documentation,12 there is an obligation by the residents of China to report changes in their Hukous to the PSB police.

A Hukou13 for the alleged address of the claimant, issued on XXXX, 1999, was submitted as evidence. The residents listed in this Hukou14 were the claimant and her son. There is a notation at the bottom of her son's page in the Hukou which states that the son moved on XXXX, 1999 to XXXX XXXX XXXX. The Hukou for this address, under the name of XXXX, XXXX XX, issued XXXX, 1998, shows no amendment to indicate that the son of the claimant moved to this address at the date mentioned and the panel draws a negative inference. There was no other Hukou submitted in evidence at the hearing today that indicated the claimant lived at any other address other than the address listed on the RIC that was found to be fraudulently obtained. The panel gives no probative value to this Hukou submitted by the claimant as accurately representing the claimant's alleged residence in China.

The claimant was asked many questions to explain the inconsistency between the address listed on her RIC, and the address given in her PIF and in testimony. The claimant stated that the address listed on the Hukou is a fixed address, and the other address where she allegedly lived from XXXX 2003 until XXXX 2007 is not a fixed address; it is temporary. The panel does not accept this explanation as plausible or reasonable and draws a negative inference. If the claimant, as alleged, lived at this address for four years, the panel does not find the address temporary and would reasonably expect a Hukou to have been presented reflecting her residence at this address.

The claimant stated in her Personal Information Form (PIF) narrative15 that she had moved in with her in-laws in 2003. When questioned where she lived in China since 2003 she said, " XXXX, XXXX XXXX, XXXX City." She stated that she lived there for four or five years but could not provide any proof that she lived at this residence. This address is consistent with evidence submitted in the PIF16 regarding her residence from XXXX 2003 until XXXX 2007. At the first sitting, the claimant indicated that she had no proof of residence because the apartment was rented. At the second sitting, the claimant produced into evidence17 a copy of the lease arrangements made between the owner and the claimant's husband, and also produced rent receipts for this residence, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX, XXXX. The evidence submitted indicates that the claimant's husband, XXXX XXXX XXXX, leased this apartment from XXXX, 2003 until XXXX, 2010. There is no indication, in the documents submitted, of the purpose of this rental, or the people who resided at this address. The receipts issued indicating payment of the rent for this property, are not in sequence with the dates of issuance and the panel finds this not plausible. If receipts are issued out of a receipt book, which appears to be the case given the numbering system, it is reasonable to assume that as receipts are issued for succeeding payments, the numbers from the receipt book would also increase. The numbers on the receipts issued appear to be random. There was no Hukou submitted for this address to indicate the residents who lived at this address, and the panel gives no probative value to the documents submitted, in terms of establishing the claimant's residence. The panel draws a negative inference from the claimant's testimony regarding her place of residence in China. There is nothing in our documentation18 to state that it is not necessary to obtain a Hukou to identify your place of residence, even if you are renting a property and living on the property.

Counsel submitted that in reality, people may not follow the procedures outlined for dealing with Hukous. However, in this case, there appears to be no credible evidence submitted as to the claimant's living address, and the panel finds the claimant not credible.

The claimant stated that the mother and father of her husband, as well as her son, lived at the address of the rental property. The claimant gave the name of her father-in-law as XXX XXX XXX and submitted, as evidence at the hearing, her father-in-law's Hukou as proof of his address. However, the address on the Hukou for her father-in-law, issued on XXXX, 1998, was: XX, XXXXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX, XXXX City. No evidence was produced at the hearing to indicate that the father-in-law's address was 2807-3-176 Binjianxi Rd., where the claimant and her in-laws allegedly moved in 2003. The panel draws a negative inference from the lack of probative evidence regarding the claimant's alleged residences from XXXX 1999 until she left China and also from the lack of evidence to support the claimant's assertion that she and her in-laws lived together. The additional evidence submitted at the second sitting does not establish the residence of the claimant or her in-laws. The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the Hukous submitted indicating the claimant's residence in China are fraudulent, in that they do not indicate that the claimant actually lived in China during the time period, from 1999 until she left China on XXXX 2008.

The claimant's PIF19 indicated that she allegedly lived at XXXX., XXXX, XXXX XXXX, XXXX, from XXXX 1998 until XXXX 2003. This address is consistent with one of the three Hukous submitted20. The claimant stated she allegedly moved into that residence in XXXX 1996, after marriage. This Hukou, presented in evidence, was issued on XXXX, 1999 and indicated that the claimant had moved into that address on XXXX, 1997. The panel draws a negative inference from the inconsistencies between the dates listed on the Hukou, PIF, and oral testimony.

The claimant stated that she, her husband, and her son lived at that address. The husband is not listed as a resident at that address. The panel also draws a negative inference from the husband not being listed on the Hukou, where he allegedly lived from 1996. Counsel submitted into evidence, an article from The UN Refugee Agency,21 dated November 7, 2002, that states, "it is possible that husband and wife, living in the same house, could have separate Hukous with one designated rural and the other urban (October 5, 2002)" According to our documentation,22 there is an obligation by Chinese citizens to report to the Hukou police any changes in address, and the names of the residents who move in or out of an address. Counsel submitted that this may be the laws of China but not necessarily the reality. Because of the many inconsistencies regarding both addresses and dates, between documents submitted in testimony, the panel accepts counsel's submission, but gives no credibility to the claimant's documents or her testimony regarding her residence in China. The claimant has not honoured her obligation to the laws regarding Hukous in China. The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant has not been a credible witness regarding her alleged residence in China.

Because of the number of negative inferences drawn on the information provided by the claimant with regards to the Hukous, the panel gives no probative value to these documents. The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the Hukous submitted do not give accurate information regarding the claimant's address of residence and finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the Hukous are fraudulent. Marriage Certificate

The claimant submitted a marriage certificate, as proof of her marriage to XXXX XXXX XXXX. There are no security features on the marriage certificate to authenticate that the document is valid. Because of previous concerns regarding the claimant's credibility, the panel gives no probative value to this document. Birth certificate

The claimant submitted for the second sitting, a birth certificate for her son, dated XXXX, 1997. There are no security features on the birth certificate to validate its authenticity. As stated earlier in these reasons, fraudulent documents are easily obtained in China. The information on the birth certificate appears to be accurate. If the document is valid, it indicates that the claimant's son was born in XXXX City on XXXX, 1997. However, there have been no valid documents regarding the claimant's alleged residence in China. The panel has found, based on the lack of credibility of the claimant regarding knowledge of the RIC, that the RIC was fraudulently obtained. The documents submitted at the hearing indicate that the claimant was in China for the birth of her son on XXXX, 1997 and give an alleged place of residence on XXXX 1999. Due to the lack of credibility and inconsistencies in documentation, there has been no valid evidence submitted that indicates the claimant was a resident of China during the time that she alleges, nor that she is a citizen of China. The claimant has not established, to the satisfaction of the panel, her identity as a Chinese national or a resident of China.

In summary, the claimant provided no reliable documentation. The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant has failed to produce sufficient credible documents and evidence to establish her identity as a national of China as required by section 106 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act and Rule 7 of the Refugee Protection Division Rules. Because identity is the first step for a person claiming refugee protection, there is no further need for the panel to assess whether the claimant in this case faces persecution or is a person in need of protection

The determinative issue in this claim is the claimant's identity. The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant is not a credible witness in this regard. On the basis that the panel cannot determine the claimant's identity, the panel is unable to determine that the claimant is a Convention refugee or that she is a person in need of protection and rejects her claim for refugee protection.
